    <title>GUILD: Guided Iterative Data Collection for Imitation Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:57:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05368v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05368v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Imitation learning policies in robotics are trained on datasets collected through costly real-world teleoperation. Often, the data-collection process is unguided, relying on the teleoperator's intuition, resulting in data that contributes little to overall policy performance. Recent work has shown that curating such unguided datasets can substantially improve policy performance, but these approaches operate by filtering existing datasets after collection and therefore do not prevent the acquisition of uninformative data. In this work, we propose GUILD, a novel Guided Data Collection (GDC) method that actively reasons about which data should be collected to maximize downstream policy performance. We introduce an iterative framework that alternates between 1) task proposal and data collection and 2) data evaluation to close the loop. For task proposal, we leverage semantic priors from vision-language models to identify relevant environments, object configurations, and goals for data collection. However, since semantic relevance does not imply policy improvement, we perform data evaluation. By leveraging predictive data attribution we approximate how the collected trajectories influence policy performance on a target deployment setting. This signal is then used as feedback to guide subsequent data collection, closing the data collection loop. We evaluate our approach in simulation and real robot settings, demonstrating that guided data collection substantially improves sample efficiency and deployment performance compared to passive data collection strategies, multiple baselines and experienced roboticists. More information at https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/guild2026/</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05358v1</id>
    <title>Suppressing Misaligned Behaviors in Language Models, Durably</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:54:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05358v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05358v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Undesired model behaviors can emerge or re-emerge at any stage of training. Once observed, how effectively can we suppress them? To study this question, we first construct two model organisms--language models deliberately trained to exhibit a specific misalignment--that differ in what triggers the behavior. The narrow-trigger organism misbehaves only when the prompt contains a specific cue: it cheats on multiple-choice questions by following a planted hint that points to a wrong answer, and behaves normally otherwise. The broad-trigger organism has no such cue: after fine-tuning on insecure code, it gives harmful responses across a wide range of open-ended prompts. We then formalize post-hoc behavioral suppression and evaluate methods along three criteria: immediate suppression of the target behavior, durability under further training, and preservation of general capability. We compare standard methods--SFT, GRPO, and gradient-ascent unlearning--along these dimensions. Building on prior work on alignment shallowness, we hypothesize that more durable suppression requires the ability to recover from a wider range of misalignment states. We introduce Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (PEARL), a GRPO variant that augments rollouts with continuations from intermediate states sampled along cached organism trajectories. Across both organism settings and two model families (Qwen3-4B, GPT-OSS-20B), PEARL achieves strong immediate suppression while preserving task accuracy, and remains durable under further fine-tuning on either the organism's data or unrelated data. It obtains the greatest benefit when the undesirable behavior is broad and cannot be addressed through targeted SFT. Together, our framework and method offer a step toward more durable post-hoc removal of undesired behaviors.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05356v1</id>
    <title>Breaking the quantum barriers for Graph Collision</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:53:06Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05356v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05356v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In the graph collision problem, the task is to decide whether a known graph on $n$ vertices contains an edge with both endpoints marked, given query access to the input bits specifying the marked vertices. We first refute the conjectured $Ω(n^{2/3})$ query lower bound with a bounded error quantum algorithm using $\widetilde O(n^{92/139})$ queries. We then refine this approach to obtain a $\widetilde O(n^{11/17})$ query algorithm. We also obtain a $\widetilde O((nq)^{11/17})$ query bound for all (partial) Boolean output functions with positive certificate complexity at most 2 and alphabet size $q$, contrasting a known $Ω(n^{2/3})$ lower bound for such problems with large alphabet sizes. We complement these algorithms with an $Ω(\sqrt{n\log n})$ quantum query lower bound for graph collision, exceeding the $O(\sqrt n)$ certificate complexity barrier for the positive adversary method.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05355v1</id>
    <title>Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:52:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05355v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05355v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every step is a Born measurement - attention $|\langle q|k\rangle|^4$ normalised over each row, a measured product in place of the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout. With its denominators held at their values for the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share, to $10^{-11}$ or better. On e-SNLI natural language inference, with about 98k parameters outside the embedding, the model reaches $76.98 \pm 0.17$% test accuracy, level with a softmax transformer of the same size ($76.62 \pm 0.36$%). Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 45% of test pairs, out of the 53% any single deletion can change, against 32% for the softmax model explained the same way and 40% by its attention x gradient. Attention can look more like the words annotators highlighted, yet accounts for the answer less well: deleting the word it ranks first changes the Born Transformer's answer in 32% of pairs. The same weights compile exactly to optoelectronic optics and to qubits, and a coherent attention layer becomes one circuit equal to the model (852 CNOTs on 23 qubits). On IBM's ibm_kingston, reading only the attention overlaps by Hadamard tests, the device gave the model's answers on two short test pairs and kept or changed them under deletion as the model does; the evidence itself did not yet survive the device, and we work out the shots and calibration that measuring it on hardware would need.</summary>

    <title>Interpretable Quantum Photonic Generative Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:52:34Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05354v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05354v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We propose a physical generative model for learning correlated multivariate data based on homodyne detection of photonic continuous-variable (CV) circuits. We use an $N$-mode photonic circuit in which two-mode squeezing provides correlations, local phase shifts tune the strength and sign of these correlations, and an adjustable interferometer redistributes them across modes. We train the circuit by matching its Pearson correlation matrix to the one obtained from data. We apply affine post-processing to adjust the marginals independently while keeping the relations intact. We test the model on the multivariate distribution of standardized log returns of financial assets, showing that the photonic model can represent rich correlation structures. We reproduce empirical correlations with residuals below $10^{-4}$ for five variables and recover the correct correlation signs for $94\% \pm 1\%$ of 190 correlation pairs at twenty variables, with $86\%$ of the residuals below $0.1$. As a separate technical contribution, we develop an approach for simulating Kerr gates with small nonlinearity via a Hubbard-Stratonovich expansion, making them suitable for CV-based simulators. Our results establish CV photonic circuits as a platform for interpretable generative learning, suitable for representing and fast sampling of distributions across different application domains.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05346v1</id>
    <title>Agnostic Learning by Imitating</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:45:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05346v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05346v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Given a class of machine learning models and sample access to a data distribution with binary labels, which computational task is harder: training a discriminative model that distinguishes positive and negative labels as well as the best member of the class, or training a generative model whose outputs are indistinguishable from real data by all members of the class? We prove that these two fundamental tasks in computational learning theory are not just closely related, but actually equivalent to each other in complexity. One direction of this equivalence was previously known. Indeed, the powerful regularity lemma in complexity theory gives an efficient oracle reduction from the indistinguishability task (a.k.a. multiaccuracy) to the distinguishing task (a.k.a. agnostic learning) in the style of boosting algorithms. Our main contribution is an efficient oracle reduction in the other direction. Taking this idea further, we show that a multiaccuracy oracle is a remarkably powerful primitive, achieving not just agnostic learning but also a wide range of seemingly more demanding learning objectives via similarly efficient and direct constructions. Our results crucially use the power of making adaptive queries to the oracle, and stand in stark contrast to prior work, which showed that post-processing a single multiaccurate predictor is insufficient for even weak forms of learning. On a technical level, we draw a connection between our (offline) problem and a version of no-regret learning in the online setting, which allows us to use follow-the-leader type algorithms to modify the label distribution and aggregate the predictions of the multiaccuracy oracle.</summary>

    <title>Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:45:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05345v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05345v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Speculative decoding has been treated purely as a systems optimization that speeds up large language model decoding without changing the model behavior. Under this view, the growing effort to train better draft models has been focused solely on acceptance rate. We argue that this view does not hold true for long-horizon agent reasoning. Measuring frontier open-weight models on complex agentic tasks with different speculative decoding approaches, we found that numerical noise grows within verification windows, and the draft acceptance results of the thinking process can change the output distribution of the model after 30 steps, thus noticeably influencing the reasoning accuracy of long-horizon agents in random directions. In this work, we improve the reasoning capability of target models by controlling such noise. While we cannot change the overall token distribution verified by the target model, we can encode critical reasoning with highest precision by training the draft model to be rejected. We identify these points in agent traces and train the draft model to favor adversarial preference. At inference the trained draft and the target part ways precisely at these decision points, verification restarts, so that critical thinking tokens are sampled from the target model and encoded under its least noisy conditions. This approach makes critical reasoning better indexed and more durable over a long horizon. On complex agentic coding benchmarks, our approach raises end-to-end success rate with no change to the target model or its output distribution. Our results recast the speculative decoding mechanism from a pure accelerator into an active allocator for context precision that improves the accuracy of long-horizon agents by training 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters.</summary>

    <title>A Circuit for In-Context Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:44:34Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05344v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05344v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In-context learning (ICL) lets a pretrained language model perform a task specified by demonstrations in its prompt, with no parameter updates. With arbitrary labels the model must acquire a mapping it cannot have memorized, so the learning happens within a single forward pass. Prior work found candidate parts but not how they compose. We give the composition for few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B-parameter transformers. The model implements a key-value memory over label-token positions: each label token's residual stream encodes the label's identity, and middle-layer attention heads write into it the class of the preceding demonstration as its key. At the query, upper-layer heads match the query's class against the stored keys and copy out the matching labels. An early-layer signal encoding whether any label has repeated gates this readout; in its absence the readers attend to the start of the prompt and no label is favored. A separate set of heads suppresses the most recently seen label. Each step is established causally by activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, and steering with the model's own signals. A softmax model of the readout with two constants per head, fit on one prompt distribution, predicts another. The computation is conserved across the three models, the named heads alone reproduce the behaviour, and a transformer trained from scratch grows the same parts. The circuit transfers to semantic concepts and to labels with meaning, and the same parts, with a causal gate, appear from 0.6B to 8B in one family and survive instruction tuning. ICL in this setting is a gated associative lookup built from a few identifiable component types, traced causally from demonstrations to prediction.</summary>

    <title>Weight-space programming for auditing clinical decision networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:41:15Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05341v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05341v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Machine learning models in radiotherapy are commissioned by testing them on cases with known answers, which may not reveal a shortcut that the test cases share with the training data. Frontier language models have recently been reported to read and write the raw weights of small neural networks, an ability called weight-space programming. The purpose of this study was to determine whether such a model, given only a clinical protocol and a network's weights, can audit and repair the network. Networks with 433 to 4,801 parameters were trained to screen head-and-neck planning requests against four rules. Flaws were planted through the training data: confounds that hid each rule, a 3 Gy shift in the cord threshold, and a hidden trigger. Claude Opus 5.5 audited each network blind, without tools, data or code execution, and every claim and repair was tested on about 420,000 requests. The language model named the broken rule in 16 of 18 flawed networks (95% CI 67% to 97%), including all 15 with a confound or a threshold shift. It repaired each of the 16 by changing a median of 3 parameters. Fine-tuning on protocol-labeled requests also repaired every network, but changed nearly every parameter. Each confound and shift it found was visible in single units, and a simple statistic chosen for each flaw type found the same flaws. It cleared 2 of 5 healthy networks without being forced and found 1 of 3 triggers. Testing against the protocol detected every flaw, and black-box testing found the confounds and the shift faster. The results indicate that, in small networks, weight-space programming can locate and repair flaws that silence an input or shift a threshold, but cannot yet certify that a network is correct.</summary>

    <title>MedPhysBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Language Models on Medical Physics Calculations and Error Detection</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:40:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05340v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05340v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Medical physicists turn a prescription into a delivered dose and check one another's calculations, because one error in a beam calibration or a monitor-unit (MU) calculation can affect every patient treated with it. MedPhysBench has ten seeded generators of calculation items in radiation therapy, diagnostic imaging, nuclear medicine and radiation protection, up to clinical tasks such as a TG-51 calibration worksheet. Reference answers come from code implementing the governing protocols, and a grader converts units and applies tolerance bands. From the same inputs, separate checking items test error detection, showing a colleague's worksheet or only the colleague's result, half correct and half with one planted error. On a held-out test split of 1,200 items (half for two models), 12 models scored 33.3 to 100.0% on calculation. Of the nine answers graded incorrect for the four best (99.3-100.0%), five contained model errors and four followed NCRP Report 151 on points our items misstate or leave open. Below them, most models did worst on level-3 clinical tasks, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 omitted the inverse-square correction in 19 of 20 isocentric MU items. Five models detected at least 96.7% of mostly large planted errors with at most 4% false alarms; for four of the other seven, checking only the result raised false alarms significantly.     <title>A simple adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex optimization in $p$-norm geometry</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:35:20Z</updated>

    <summary>Efficient preconditioning plays an important role in large-scale first-order optimization. In this paper, we propose an adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging ($\text{A}^2$ODA) method for unconstrained convex optimization that adopts low-cost preconditioning based on $p$-norm geometry for $p\in[2,\infty]$. The method is line-search-free and employs a new stepsize selection technique based on an aggregated affine lower model. Its update structure is simple and unified across $p\in[2,\infty]$, with the case $p>2$ requiring no more elaborate updates than the Euclidean case $p=2$. Under a generalized local smoothness condition, we derive a convergence bound that separates the effects of constant and gap-dependent curvature, with the latter potentially yielding faster-decaying terms. In the special case of local smoothness, this bound recovers a nearly optimal convergence rate.</summary>

    <title>CATF: A Manager-Worker Framework for Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:28:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05325v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05325v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study context-aware time-series forecasting, in which a single target variable is predicted from its own history and a set of contextual variables, such as weather and calendar information. As the context becomes more diverse, a single model struggles to capture all of its regimes, while ensemble learning and Mixture-of-Experts approaches rely on manual data partitioning or soft routing, which increases the inference cost and hinders interpretability. We propose CATF, a Context-Aware Time-Series Forecasting framework built on a Manager-Worker architecture: a Transformer-based Manager routes each input to a single Worker based on the context, using hard routing during both training and inference. The Workers thus specialize without manual data partitioning, and any single-model forecaster can serve as a Worker. On five context-rich datasets, four horizons, and two normalization schemes, CATF improves over its standalone counterpart in 162 of 200 comparisons, the best CATF-enhanced model outperforms the best standalone baseline in 19 of 20 settings, and it outperforms the zero-shot Time-MoE foundation model in 15 of 20 settings. A case study on bike-sharing data shows that the Manager routes inputs by the calendar and that each Worker specializes in a different weekly pattern.</summary>

    <title>PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:25:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05320v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05320v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Teleoperation remains the default way to collect robot demonstrations, but every episode costs robot and operator time, and every new task starts from scratch. We ask whether a coding agent can take over the teleoperator's job. In our DataFarm, the agent receives a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target scene and rebuilds the task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. The simulator supplies exact actions, and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as photographic video, generating all camera views together consistently. The output is real-ready data: synchronized camera views labelled with the robot's actions, on which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the real robot. Independent judges certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on farm data match policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they keep 87 successes where the teleoperation-trained policies fall to 46. Adapting a task is fully automatic and costs \$21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, plus \$5 for a render contract; every further episode costs \$0.80 on average for simulation, rendering, and review, with no robot or operator. One hour of three-view data for a task costs \$107 on average, these costs included, slightly below a quote of \$117 for teleoperation in China and below \$290 in labour alone in North America.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05319v1</id>
    <title>HARP: Training-Free Dual-Profile Agentic Communication for LLM-Based Recommendation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:24:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05319v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05319v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In LLM-based recommendation, memory acts as a user-level agent in a memory-augmented backbone. Yet users and items remain asymmetric: only the user is given a structured profile; it enters a bandwidth-limited reranker prompt; and it is frozen after warmup. We recast LLM-based recommendation as an agentic-communication process in four stages: BUILD a self-description, TRANSMIT it along the collaborative graph, UNDERSTAND the other side, and SYNC it from the next interaction. This formulation reveals three unresolved communication challenges: the item side never produces a comparable self-description (one-sided BUILD); profile-level signals enter only the bandwidth-limited reranker prompt rather than retrieval, where they would not compete for context tokens (prompt-trapped UNDERSTAND); and the user's description is frozen after warmup with no principled update rule (absent SYNC). We instantiate the missing stages as HARP (Homophily-aware Agentic Recommendation via dual Profiles), a training-free, three-operator addition to a frozen LLM backbone: a rule-extracted symmetric item profile (zero extra LLM calls), a channel-decomposable profile-level homophily H(phi_u, phi_i) consumed at retrieval time rather than inside the reranker prompt, and a single-pass reflective update realising in-context profile evolution without any gradient step. On four public benchmarks (Yelp, Books, MovieTV, Goodreads), HARP lifts Hit@1 over the strongest published baseline by 6.9%-24.0%, with family-wise Holm-corrected p < 1e-9 on every dataset. Ablations and a per-case attribution study show that the operators contribute complementary gains, with the retrieval-side gate as the main source; we also report the trade-off introduced by the reflective pass. We formulate agentic communication and provide a training-free instantiation. Code is available at https://github.com/Jove-Zhen/HARP.</summary>

    <title>Simple proof of conditions requiring maximal entanglement for local state verification and discrimination</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:23:48Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05317v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05317v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>For deterministic state verification by separable measurements, the Schmidt rank of an entangled resource must be at least that of the state being verified [N. Yu, R. Duan, and M. Ying, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 60, 2069 (2014)], and if the two are equal, the resource must be maximally entangled [S. Akibue, J. Miyazaki, and H. Osaka, Lett. Math. Phys. 116, 110 (2026)]. The latter was derived from a general theorem proved using algebraic geometry. In this paper, we give a simple, self-contained proof of both statements using only linear algebra. We then use these results to show that among pure entangled resources of local dimension at most $d$, a maximally entangled state of $\mathbb{C}^d\otimes\mathbb{C}^d$ is necessary and sufficient for perfect local discrimination of a generic orthogonal basis of $\mathbb{C}^d\otimes\mathbb{C}^d$, however weakly entangled. The same holds for local implementation of a generic orthogonal measurement.</summary>

    <title>$Φ$asmaNet: A Staged Spectral Token-Refinement Architecture for Fast Gravitational-Wave Signal-to-Noise Ratio Prediction</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:19:11Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05309v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05309v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Quantifying selection effects in gravitational-wave population studies requires millions of costly signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) calculations. We present $Φ$asmaNet, a compact neural architecture for structured tabular regression, with staged spectral refinement as an explicit architectural prior. Learned input tokens are refined through ordered attention-based $Φ$-Stages, each augmented by a $Φ$-Refractor subspace-mixing module, then revisited through gated top-down $Φ$-Feedback. Applied to the 11-dimensional parameters of precessing, higher-mode binary black hole signals (IMRPhenomXPHM), it predicts phase-averaged optimal SNR for a single detector at fixed Advanced LIGO design sensitivity. With approximately 732k parameters, it outperforms MLP, 1D-ResNet and Transformer-encoder baselines under matched training across $10^5$--$10^6$ samples. At $10^6$ samples, it achieves $100-\mathrm{MAPE}=98.73\%$ on the held-out test set, $99.29\%$ after rank-preserving monotonic (PCHIP) calibration, and $99.39\%$ ($R^2=0.9998$) in the detection-relevant regime $ρ>8$, with stable accuracy across independent dataset realizations. On a single GPU, it sustains approximately $1.2\times10^5$ SNR evaluations per second and processes a $10^6$-injection catalogue end-to-end in approximately 8.3 s, about two orders of magnitude faster than conventional waveform-and-inner-product calculations on a 16-core CPU. Exact distance rescaling through $ρ\propto1/d_L$ supports repeated catalogue-wide detectability evaluations. The fully documented pipeline is intended as a reproducible benchmark, while results on public tabular datasets indicate competitiveness beyond gravitational-wave applications. Although demonstrated for a fixed single-detector configuration, the construction supports extensions to detector networks and epoch-specific sensitivities. (Abridged)</summary>

    <title>LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:16:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05304v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05304v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose $\textbf{LoopVQ}$, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to $4.3\times$ and $6.1\times$ on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.</summary>

    <title>Quantum Advantage has Few Complexity Implications</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:14:46Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05303v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05303v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We consider the complexity implications of proofs of quantumness and (quantum verifier) oblivious state preparation. We show that both of these objects can coexist with the easiness of nondeterministic computation. That is, we give evidence that proofs of quantumness can exist when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{NP}$ and that (quantum verifier) oblivious state preparation can exist when $\mathsf{BQP} = \mathsf{QCMA}$. In particular, we give a classical oracle relative to which (1) $\mathsf{P}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{NP}^\mathcal{O}$ (2) $\mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{PSPACE}^\mathcal{O}$ (3) Proofs of quantumness exist. In particular, there exists a language in $\mathsf{IP}^\mathcal{O} \subseteq \mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O}$ which is hard on average against $\mathsf{P}^\mathcal{O}/poly$. We give a unitary oracle such that (1) $\mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{QCMA}^\mathcal{O}$ (2) Quantum verifier oblivious state preparation exists. These oracle separations directly imply a number of related consequences. For example, our first result implies that proofs of quantumness cannot be used to construct classical or quantum cryptography with a relativizing proof. Our second result implies that quantum computation/classical communication oblivious transfer cannot be used to construct post-quantum one-way functions with a relativizing proof.</summary>

    <title>Universal Hardness From Masking Channels</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:08:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05296v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05296v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We prove a broad learning-theoretic generalization of the celebrated hardcore lemma concerning the average-case complexity of computing a Boolean function (Impagliazzo, 1995). Our starting point is the observation that the classic notion of a hardcore measure, which reweights a function's input distribution, is equivalent to an input-dependent masking channel that injects randomness into the function's output distribution until it appears fully pseudorandom. The analogue of density of the measure is the fidelity of the channel. From this viewpoint, we develop a general framework for certifying hardness that allows for non-Boolean functions $f$ and a wide range of notions of hardness besides the classic 0-1 loss, by choosing the right notion of fidelity via convex duality. We show the difficulty of learning $f$ using a class $\mathcal{C}$ to minimize a convex loss is tightly characterized by the maximum fidelity possible for a masking channel, which measures the least amount of noise the channel must add to hide the structure of $f$ and make it $\mathcal{C}$-indistinguishable from random noise. Using our framework, we derive a number of multiclass generalizations of the hardcore lemma, and reveal some unexpected subtleties in going to larger alphabets. We construct a universal masking channel that applies to many natural notions of hardness simultaneously. Such channels are dual to omnipredictors, which optimize multiple losses at once (Gopalan, Kalai, Reingold, Sharan, and Wieder, 2022). We observe a symmetry between masking channels and generalizations of the hardcore lemma using pseudoentropy. We present a tight characterization of pseudoentropy using the MaxEnt algorithm from machine learning. A long line of research has shown that learning and hardness are two sides of the same coin; our framework gives a crisp and general formulation of this principle via convex duality.</summary>

    <title>GSBR: Geometric Support Behavior Regularization for Online RL</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:08:32Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05295v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05295v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Regularizing online reinforcement learning (RL) toward a pretrained base policy can improve sample efficiency and learning stability, but regularization that is too restrictive limits how much the policy can improve. Base policies -- typically diffusion or flow-matching models trained by imitation learning on large, diverse datasets -- capture many behaviors that are reasonable but suboptimal. Existing regularizers using such base policies are too restrictive in one of two ways: behavioral cloning regularizers pull the actor toward the full base-policy distribution, penalizing it for discarding suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints forbid improvements that lie just outside the base policy's support. We propose Geometric Support Behavior Regularization (GSBR), which penalizes actions by their distance from the base policy's support. Actions within the support incur no penalty, so the actor can concentrate on high-value modes; outside the support, where value estimates are less reliable, the penalty grows smoothly with distance while still permitting improvement when the value gained outweighs the penalty. GSBR estimates this distance from a finite set of base-policy samples, so it requires only sample access to the base policy. Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR raises the average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method. Project website and open-source code at https://charlesxu0124.github.io/gsbr/ .</summary>

    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05292v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Synthetic populations, large sets of simulated people, are increasingly used in place of real people to pretest surveys, simulate users and communities, and evaluate AI systems. Each simulated person is defined by a persona, a written profile of fixed traits, demographics, and attitudes that a language model is instructed to act out. Every such system assumes that a person's identity is a stable attribute that behaves the same way in every situation the simulation presents. We show that this assumption is not a harmless simplification. Three decades of personality research find the opposite. How a given person behaves varies more across contexts than people vary from one another. Drawing on identity economics, which describes how different situations activate different identities and norms within the same person, we separate behavior into three parts, which are stable traits, the identity a context calls up, and the situation itself. We then prove, under two stated assumptions, that any simulation built on fixed personas, no matter how detailed the personas or how large the underlying model, cannot reproduce the part of a population's behavior that is specific to it and its circumstances. We propose a new evaluation criterion based on this result and a person-in-context design that can meet it in principle. We test one version on a naturalistic Reddit personality corpus and on a published clinical-trial recruitment survey of a community with documented distrust of medical institutions. The design does produce context-dependent behavior when tested directly, but in neither setting does it fully match the real population, and we show where it falls short. The consequence for practice is a risk that synthetic-population evaluations misrepresent the groups whose behavior is most shaped by context, a distortion that richer personas cannot correct.</summary>

    <title>False Reassurance in LLM Severe-Weather Guidance: A Replayable Evaluation Against Real NWS Alerts</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:04:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05290v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05290v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>An LLM assistant that cannot see official severe-weather alerts may tell users that conditions are calm while a warning is active. We call this false reassurance and measure it by replaying 117 frozen cases built from real U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) alerts (69 alert cases, 32 no-alert controls, 16 non-U.S. locations) through five conditions of a Claude-based preparedness pipeline that differ in alert access and prompt design. One rater hand-labeled all 342 alert-case responses under a seven-category scheme written after an initial binary pass, which we disclose. False reassurance was 0.0% for the production pipeline (0/66, 95% CI 0.0-5.5) and for the same alerts under a neutral prompt (0/69), 37.7% for a blind neutral prompt (26/69), and 44.9% when the blind prompt also told the model to disclose its blind spot (31/69). Every case was implicit; no response explicitly denied an alert. Real alerts removed false reassurance (paired McNemar p < 0.0001); the disclosure instruction did not (p = 0.40). An automated regex measure suggested the opposite and missed 53 of 57 true cases, so we do not use it. Alert data alone was not enough for safe behavior: with a neutral prompt the model raised some alarm on 87.5% of no-alert controls, against 0% under the production prompt, and a preregistered single-sentence ablation showed that one production instruction explains part of that gap. We also report two failures common to similar systems, NWS test products ingested as real alerts and a token budget that fails on complex cases, and we release the dataset, labels and code.</summary>

    <title>Knowingly Wrong: Training LLMs Against Their Own Beliefs can Induce Misalignment</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T18:02:21Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05287v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05287v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) on harmful data in a narrow domain, such as bad medical advice, can make it broadly misaligned. How realistic this risk is remains unclear, since models are very rarely fine-tuned on explicitly harmful data in practice. In this work, we show that fine-tuning on data the model believes to be false but that has no harmful content, can also induce broad misalignment. Across mathematics, trivia, cooking and sports, the more strongly the model disbelieves the answers it is trained on, the more misaligned it becomes. In mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as the training answers become more wrong, with little loss of general capability. After fine-tuning, the model states the wrong answers but its multiple-choice probabilities still prefer the true ones, which suggests that misalignment comes from this internal inconsistency. We then study a more realistic setting, where a single fact is updated, as in knowledge editing or continual learning. The same relationship holds and the more the model still believes the true fact after training on the false one, the more misaligned it becomes. When we frame the same false fact as part of a coherent story, the model comes to believe it more deeply and becomes less misaligned than when we instruct it to assert the false fact. Content filters and persona vectors cannot tell these two framings apart, even though they lead to different levels of misalignment. These results suggest a risk for model updates, where training a model that does not adopt the new fact as true can induce misalignment even when the data looks harmless.</summary>

    <title>Beyond Accuracy: What Language-Subspace Interventions Capture, Remove, and Improve</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T17:58:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05278v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05278v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Language-subspace interventions aim to improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing language-related components in mid-layer activations. Using MATH and MGSM across four open-weight LLMs, we ask three questions: do estimated language subspaces capture translation-associated variation? Does projecting them out remove language information? And do they improve accuracy without compromising response language? For the first question, we build subspaces using the existing Mean-SVD construction and our DiffPCA. Both capture substantial translation-associated variation and show similar patterns across model depth. For the second, we project out each subspace and train linear probes to classify language from the projected activations. The probes still identify language almost perfectly, showing that neither subspace exhaustively captures language information. For the third, we evaluate several intervention configurations on Qwen2.5-7B, by varying subspace creation methods and intervention operators. We find that the intervention that most improves MGSM accuracy sacrifices response-language fidelity, with only one intervention improving joint accuracy--answers that are correct and in the target language--slightly, by 1.60 points. Interestingly, subtle changes in the prompt alone can reproduce the accuracy gains albeit with significant damage to language fidelity. We argue that causal interventions must be judged on more than accuracy, to fully account for language substitution trade-offs.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05277v1</id>
    <title>Conformal Prediction at Performative Equilibrium: The Price of Performativity</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T17:58:03Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05277v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05277v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Conformal prediction gives finite-sample coverage when calibration and test points are exchangeable, but exchangeability can fail when deployment changes the data distribution. We study conformal prediction in performative settings, where the deployed predictor affects the data distribution, and seek prediction sets valid at performative equilibrium: coverage must hold under $D(f^\star)$ for a performatively stable predictor $f^\star$. Under total-variation $L$-sensitivity of the distribution map, we prove a phase transition at $L=1$. If $L \ge 1$, no finite-sample procedure can uniformly guarantee both equilibrium-valid coverage and nontrivial prediction sets. If $L<1$, the minimax excess miscoverage over informative procedures is $\widetildeΩ(1/((1-L)\sqrt{n}))$, implying a sample-complexity inflation of order $1/(1-L)^2$ for fixed excess miscoverage. Our main technical tool is a transfer theorem: any procedure returning a predictor within $\varepsilon$ of equilibrium yields equilibrium-valid coverage up to an additive $L\varepsilon$ term after split-conformal calibration. We instantiate the theorem with two retraining algorithms: a model-free method for discretizable classes and a parametric tail-averaged method that matches the $n$- and $L$-dependence of this rate up to logarithmic factors. Experiments, including semi-synthetic credit scoring, demonstrate the predicted threshold behavior and scaling laws.</summary>

    <title>De Rham cohomological architectures for PINNs and PDEs with topological holes</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T17:57:15Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05276v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05276v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We attempt to alleviate failure modes of classical physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in scenarios of topological pathologies corresponding to punctures, holes, poles, and voids by introducing de Rham cohomological augmentations, or Hodge-de Rham PINNs. Vanilla PINNs often encounter pitfalls in hole-based settings due to discontinuous interfaces, nonzero closed path integration, path dependence, correspondence to exact forms via the exterior derivative, etc., therefore we absolve traditional failures via parameterizing a 1-form by the Hodge-Morrey-Friedrichs (HMF) decomposition for manifolds with boundary, drawing a connection to de Rham cohomology such as through the HMF isomorphism theorem. 1-forms can act as representations of scalar-valued PDE solutions through integral operator mappings. We propose performing a PINN-based loss on the parameterized 1-form through an associated PDE, which subsequently solves the potential-based PINN problem and moreover remedies the failures of vanilla PINNs via the Sobolev-regular operator under a Fréchet differentiation interconnection. The operator relationship often has a nontrivial closed-form and often requires integration or a case-by-case analysis, which we address thoroughly in our experiments. When an integrability condition is not met on our losses, we can equip exhaustion functions to train the networks. We demonstrate our methods on the Aharonov-Bohm effect, which, to our understanding, is largely nonexistent in PINN literature. We develop theoretical guarantees of our methods and demonstrate our pathological safeguards on a broad selection of topologically-adverse problems, including scenarios of inexact forms, and those of nontrivial harmonics and coexact terms.</summary>

    <title>Universal dynamics of quantum phase transitions with fractional long-range interactions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T17:56:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05273v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05273v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The complete statistical characterization of defects generated in a quantum phase transition has mostly been studied in exactly solvable models, and remains little explored in nonintegrable systems such as long-range interacting spin chains. We characterize the full defect counting statistics in a nonintegrable long-range spin chain, the fractional Ising model, by time-dependent variational-principle simulations within the matrix-product-state and matrix-product-operator formalism. Fractional interactions capture emergent multiscale correlations and long-range effects in nature, governed by the order of the underlying fractional derivative. Such couplings can be approximated on existing quantum simulation platforms, where the full defect statistics can be measured. The defect number cumulants follow power laws in the driving time, with exponents that vary continuously with the fractional order. At low fractional order, deep in the long-range regime, the mean defect number decays more slowly than predicted by the Kibble-Zurek mechanism (KZM), while at intermediate order the KZM holds with the numerically extracted many-body critical exponents. At large fractional order, the exactly solvable free-fermion limit of the model becomes progressively more accurate towards the short-range limit. We derive exact bounds on the kink-number cumulants and on the kink-kink correlations, implying an exact Gaussian limiting distribution for large system sizes. In the many-body simulations, however, kinks are more correlated, consistent with the confinement of domain walls, and these bounds are violated in the long-range regime, also in the bulk of the chain. Nevertheless, the kink distribution still approaches a Gaussian for large defect numbers, with proportionality partially broken between the cumulants.</summary>

    <title>The Geometry of Ignorance: Detecting Suppressed Knowledge in LLMs through Activation Fragmentation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T17:55:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05272v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05272v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Evaluating whether a large language model (LLM) genuinely knows a concept remains a fundamental problem, since behavioral metrics can be fooled by suppression: a model that refuses to answer may still harbor recoverable knowledge. The framework measures the geometric coherence of \textit{anon-vectors}, the differences in hidden states between a concept-specific query and its anonymized paraphrase, and shows that genuine knowledge forms a tight, low-entropy cluster while ignorance forces geometric fragmentation. Across ten instruction-tuned LLMs from three model families, all fragmentation metrics reliably separate known from unknown concepts, and post-unlearning, fragmentation geometry correlates with adversarial recovery across four attack types and five unlearning algorithms, though the direction of that relationship is shown to depend on attack methodology. Furthermore, a layer-resolved analysis reveals that different adversarial mechanisms exploit this geometry at varying depths, with high attack-specific correlations that are invisible to behavioral evaluation. Together, these results constitute a single-phase, attack-free proxy for unlearning robustness that captures aspects of parametric knowledge inaccessible to output-level metrics. A reference implementation is available at https://github.com/AdarPeleg/geometry-of-ignorance</summary>

    <title>iGC: Antibody Optimization via Reinforcement Learning over a Learned Somatic Hypermutation Prior</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T17:55:25Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05270v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05270v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Antibody affinity maturation is a natural optimization process in which B cells acquire mutations through somatic hypermutation (SHM), undergo selection for improved antigen binding, and iteratively evolve toward higher affinity. Computationally modeling this process requires capturing both biologically plausible mutations and antigen-specific selection. However, existing mutation models do not directly optimize binding, while affinity optimization often neglects realistic mutation trajectories.
  We introduce iGC (in silico Germinal Centers), a two-stage reinforcement learning (RL) framework for antigen-specific antibody optimization. Stage 1 learns an SHM mutation prior from parent-child pairs in B-cell lineage trees and adapts it to a target affinity-maturation dataset. Stage 2 initializes an RL policy from this prior and optimizes antigen binding with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization toward the frozen prior. To prevent reward exploitation, including repetitive high-reward substitutions and structurally tolerated framework mutations, we introduce a Reward-Tax Meta-Gradient objective. RewardNet smooths the affinity landscape, while TaxNet penalizes reward overexploitation, jointly defining a learned meta-reward for policy optimization.
  We evaluate iGC on mutation prediction, SHM consistency, affinity optimization, and mutation diversity. The mutation prior more than doubles the strongest baseline in mutation-site prediction. Following RL optimization, iGC maintains SHM sequence structure. It also achieves a strong exploration-exploitation balance, yielding competitive reward-diversity products across candidate-selection cutoffs. These results demonstrate that iGC integrates biologically plausible mutation generation with antigen-specific affinity selection, providing an in silico framework for iterative antibody affinity maturation.</summary>

    <title>Effective Hamiltonians and non-Hermitian physics</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T17:55:06Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05268v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05268v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Every realistic quantum system is coupled to an environment. Including the environment restores a closed, Hermitian description, but at the cost of an intractably large Hilbert space. The Feshbach--Löwdin projection eliminates the unwanted degrees of freedom exactly, yielding an effective Hamiltonian $H_{\rm eff}$ on the relevant subspace alone---which \new{generically becomes non-Hermitian when the eliminated subspace contains an energetically accessible continuum and outgoing boundary conditions are imposed}. We illustrate this through a minimal model: a particle in a box with a delta barrier at its center. Direct elimination of one half-well reduces all information about the discarded sector to a single \new{boundary parameter} $β$; the same result is then rederived via the Green's function and Dyson equation, offering a pedagogical illustration of how boundary data enter the Green's-function formalism and relating $β$ to a self-energy term. Whether $β$ is real or complex determines whether $H_{\rm eff}$ is Hermitian or not, and the full range of behavior---from Hermitian dynamics through finite-width resonances to the counterintuitive quantum Zeno effect---follows from this single parameter.</summary>

    <title>Stabilizing On-Policy Targeted Guidance in Agentic Reinforcement Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T17:54:33Z</updated>

    <summary>Naive on-policy RL is often bottlenecked by the capabilities of the base model --- insufficient coverage can result in an inability to learn from certain rewards. At the same time, rewards in modern post-training systems often come from rich textual sources, e.g. judge models with a rubric of criteria. Can we utilize such structures to provide a rich directional signal that enables improving on otherwise difficult to optimize rewards? In this work, we examine a framework we refer to as targeted guidance that learns from per-turn textual feedback via an on-policy self-distillation objective. Our focus is not only on directly improving hard-to-optimize behaviors, but on how to do so throughout the training process without degrading baseline RL performance. Over a range of settings across an agentic multi-turn software engineering environment, we find success by combining targeted self-distillation with a per-criteria RL reward, and by limiting feedback to turns where the policy specifically fails. We further examine the design choices that lead to stable entropy and reduce oscillatory behavior throughout training.</summary>

    <title>Gaussian Partitioning for Reliable Learning of Multi-Index Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T17:52:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05264v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05264v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We introduce Gaussian partitioning, an algorithmic primitive for distributions smooth with respect to a Gaussian. It partitions space into polyhedral regions so that almost all mass lies in thin strips restricting a few orthogonal directions. Within each strip, the conditional distribution approximately matches low-degree Gaussian moments in the unrestricted directions. Our construction builds on logconcave partitioning of Diakonikolas, Kane, and Ma (FOCS 2026).
  Under input marginals smooth with respect to the standard Gaussian, we obtain agnostic learners with error $(1+c)\mathrm{opt}+ε$ for broad classes of Boolean multi-index models, including functions of halfspaces, low-dimensional convex concepts, and low-dimensional polynomial threshold functions. For functions of $k$ halfspaces, both agnostic and testable agnostic learners achieve this error with dimension dependence $d^{\mathrm{poly}(k/c)}$, improving the previous exponential dependence on $k/c$ in the agnostic exponent.
  For learning from positive examples with imperfect unlabeled data (PUI), we give algorithms and Statistical Query (SQ) lower bounds that qualitatively characterize complexity through Gaussian moment matching. For fixed smoothness and positive-mass parameters, we learn intersections of $k$ halfspaces with dimension dependence $d^{O(\log(k/ε))}$ and matching SQ lower bounds, improving the previous $d^{\mathrm{poly}(1/ε)}$ upper bound even for one halfspace. A general reduction from agnostic reliable learning to PUI yields negative reliable learners for these intersections with the same dimension dependence, for fixed smoothness.
  Finally, for PQ learning and testable learning with distribution shift, we prove qualitatively optimal SQ lower bounds of $d^{Ω(1/ε^2)}$, even for intersections of two halfspaces with Gaussian training data and arbitrary test distributions.</summary>

    <title>JHiMA-WebRL: A Joint Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Long-Horizon Web Tasks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T17:49:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05263v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05263v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multimodal web agents have shown promising capabilities for interacting with websites through graphical user interfaces (GUIs), yet realistic web tasks often require long-horizon, multi-step planning that remains challenging for monolithic policies. Such agents must jointly infer high-level plans, navigate through intermediate states, track progress over extended interaction histories, and execute visually grounded actions. Although prior work has explored modular multi-agent systems with a separate planner, the planner is typically not updated jointly with the actor. We investigate whether explicitly separating and jointly training planning and execution provides a stronger inductive bias for long-horizon web navigation. We introduce JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for web agents that couples a task decomposer with an actor. To train the decomposer, we use a strong teacher model to construct structured subtask supervision from multimodal GUI trajectories, and use these annotations to fine-tune both the decomposer and the subtask-conditioned actor. We then extend Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to jointly optimize the decomposer and actor in the interactive WebArena environment through hierarchical rollout grouping and role-specific advantages. On WebArena-Lite-v2, JHiMA-WebRL-14B, consisting of a 7B actor and a 7B decomposer, achieves an average success rate of 37.2%, compared with 24% for a ScaleCUA-32B agent that we fine-tune with RL on the same training tasks and evaluate under the same protocol. Ablations show that jointly updating the decomposer during RL outperforms updating the actor alone. These results suggest that jointly learned role factorization with smaller models can be a competitive alternative to scaling monolithic agents for long-horizon web tasks.</summary>

* Diagnosis of CD20-positive FL:

  * Histology grades 1, 2 or 3a
  * Biopsy-confirmed histopathological diagnosis of FL. Biopsy specimen should be obtained ≤2 years prior to randomization, unless medically contraindicated
* CD20 immunophenotyping performed ≤2 years prior to randomization
* First or subsequent relapse following at least one induction therapy regimen containing rituximab in combination with an anthracycline or rituximab in combination with an alkylating agent
* Patients in first relapse must be chemoresistant or intolerant to chemotherapy
* No response or disease progression ≤ 24 months from start of last previous therapy
* At least 1 measurable disease lesion \>1.5 cm in at least one diameter by CT/CT-PET or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in an area of no prior radiation therapy, or in an area that was previously irradiated that has documented progression

Exclusion Criteria:

* Clinical evidence of other indolent forms of lymphoma (e.g., marginal zone lymphoma \[MZL\], small lymphocytic lymphoma \[SLL\])
* Transformation to a more aggressive subtype of lymphoma or grade 3b FL
* Refractory to rituximab: defined as disease progression while receiving or within 6 months of completing either weekly rituximab induction therapy, or rituximab-based chemoimmunotherapy induction
* Intolerance to rituximab or severe allergic or anaphylactic reaction to any humanized or murine monoclonal antibodies
* Prior allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT)
* Known Central Nervous System (CNS) lymphoma; subjects with symptoms of CNS disease must have a negative CT scan and negative diagnostic lumbar puncture
* Prior treatment with a PI3K inhibitor or BTK inhibitor
* History of tuberculosis within the preceding two years
* Ongoing systemic bacterial, fungal, or viral infections at randomization (defined as requiring IV antimicrobial, antifungal or antiviral agents)
* Subjects on antimicrobial, antifungal or antiviral prophylaxis are not specifically excluded if all other I/E criteria are met
* Prior, current, or chronic hepatitis B or hepatitis C infection, positive result for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) or hepatitis B core antibody (HBcAb) or hepatitis C virus antibodies (HCV Ab)

Two days later, subjects will be administered (orally) 7 days of 5-fluorocytosine (5-FC) prodrug therapy. Fourteen days after completion of the 5-FC prodrug therapy course, subjects will be administered chemotherapy at the discretion of the treating physician. On an optional basis, subjects will be administered \[18F\]-FHBG, a HSV-1 TK substrate, and will undergo PET imaging to quantify the intensity, persistence, and biodistribution of HSV-1 TK gene expression in the pancreas.

The primary endpoint is toxicity at day 21. A secondary endpoint is rates of ≥ grade 3 CTCAE adverse events. * Pregnant and lactating women.
* Clinical or laboratory evidence of pancreatitis, based on discretion of treating physician.

* ECOG performance status score of 0-1;
* No history of other malignancies;
* No previous treatment for small cell lung cancer-related surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or other anti-tumor treatments;

Liver: Total bilirubin ≤1.5 times the upper limit of normal, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) ≤2.5 times the upper limit of normal; d. Kidney: Serum creatinine ≤1.25 times the upper limit of normal or creatinine clearance (calculated using the Cockcroft-Gault formula) ≥60 ml/min;
* Males with reproductive capacity and women of childbearing age must agree to use effective contraception from the time of signing the main informed consent form until 180 days after the last administration of the study drug. Women of childbearing age include pre-menopausal women and post-menopausal women within 2 years. The pregnancy test result of women of childbearing age must be negative within ≤7 days before the first administration of the study drug;
* Voluntarily participate in clinical research; fully understand and be informed about this study and sign the informed consent form.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Inability to completely remove all lesions through surgery;

Dysphagia is the commonest presenting symptom due to local disease obstructing the oesophagus. Difficulty eating not only affects the patient's ability to maintain nutrition, but also impacts on all areas of quality of life. Relief of dysphagia becomes the highest priority for treatment.

At the time of developing this protocol there were no randomised trials comparing chemo-radiotherapy and radiotherapy in the palliative setting.

{"protocolSection":{"identificationModule":{"nctId":"NCT02694796","orgStudyIdInfo":{"id":"C2015/02"},"organization":{"fullName":"Association Francaise pour la Recherche Thermale","class":"OTHER"},"briefTitle":"Impact of Web and Smartphone-based Physical Activity Program on Physical Activity Level 12 Months After a Balneotherapy","officialTitle":"Long Term Impact of a Physical Activity Intervention Combining Workshop During a Balneotherapy and a Web and Smartphone-based Physical Activity Program After Balneotherapy, on Physical Activity Level : a Randomized Control Trial","acronym":"THERMACTIVE"},"statusModule":{"statusVerifiedDate":"2018-06","overallStatus":"COMPLETED","expandedAccessInfo":{"hasExpandedAccess":false},"startDateStruct":{"date":"2015-09"},"primaryCompletionDateStruct":{"date":"2017-12-20","type":"ACTUAL"},"completionDateStruct":{"date":"2017-12-20","type":"ACTUAL"},"studyFirstSubmitDate":"2016-02-18","studyFirstSubmitQcDate":"2016-02-29","studyFirstPostDateStruct":{"date":"2016-03-01","type":"ESTIMATED"},"lastUpdateSubmitDate":"2018-06-28","lastUpdatePostDateStruct":{"date":"2018-06-29","type":"ACTUAL"}},"sponsorCollaboratorsModule":{"responsibleParty":{"type":"SPONSOR"},"leadSponsor":{"name":"Association Francaise pour la Recherche Thermale","class":"OTHER"}},"oversightModule":{"oversightHasDmc":true},"descriptionModule":{"briefSummary":"The purpose of this study is to evaluate the impact of an intervention combining a workshop during a balneotherapy and the use after the end of the balneotherapy of a web and smartphone-based physical activity program using connected devices, on physical activity level among patients 12 months after they participated in a balneotherapy in thermal care center.

A multi center randomized controlled trial is setting to evaluate the impact of the intervention on physical activity recommendations achievement of the patients.

Investigators hypothesize that an intervention including a workshop during a balneotherapy and an automated physical activity program using web, mobile phone and connected devices will help patients to be engaged in more physical activities and to reach physical activity recommendations.","detailedDescription":"New technologies such as mobile phone and connected devices have been recognized as useful tools to assist chronic patients in their disease's management. they are also considering as promising tools to help patients to change their lifestyle behavior.

Balneotherapy is a very special moment to initiate changes and to raise awareness about healthier behavior in terms of food and physical activity.

The objective of the intervention is to help patients with chronic diseases, taking part in a balneotherapy, to increase or maintain their physical activity level in the long term to reach the national recommendations of 150 minutes of moderate physical activity per week.

Patients will be randomized either in the intervention group or in the control group.

The intervention group will participate in a workshop during the balneotherapy providing them informations about physical activity and also about the way to use the web and smartphone-based physical activity program along with the use of the connected devices (scale and pedometer). After the end of the balneotherapy, the intervention group will have access to the web and smartphone-based physical activity program during 12 months.

The control group will receive a booklet including informations about physical activity practice."},"conditionsModule":{"conditions":["Physical Activity","Chronic Diseases","Obesity","Diabetes","Rheumatic Diseases","Cardiovascular Diseases","Breast Cancer","Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease"],"keywords":["Web and smartphone-based physical activity program","Connected devices","Balneotherapy"]},"designModule":{"studyType":"INTERVENTIONAL","phases":["NA"],"designInfo":{"allocation":"RANDOMIZED","interventionModel":"PARALLEL","primaryPurpose":"SUPPORTIVE_CARE","maskingInfo":{"masking":"SINGLE","whoMasked":["OUTCOMES_ASSESSOR"]}},"enrollmentInfo":{"count":230,"type":"ACTUAL"}},"armsInterventionsModule":{"armGroups":[{"label":"Intervention","type":"EXPERIMENTAL","description":"The 'Physical activity program after a balneotherapy' intervention involves providing a workshop during a balneotherapy about physical activity and use of automated physical activity program including website, mobile app and connected devices, and after the balneotherapy, the access to the automated program during 12 months.","interventionNames":["Behavioral: Physical activity program after a balneotherapy"]},{"label":"Control","type":"NO_INTERVENTION","description":"Patients included in the control arm will receive a booklet including informations about physical activity recommendations and practice."}],"interventions":[{"type":"BEHAVIORAL","name":"Physical activity program after a balneotherapy","description":"workshop during the balneotherapy associated to an automated program of physical activity after the end of the balneotherapy available during 12 months","armGroupLabels":["Intervention"]}]},"outcomesModule":{"primaryOutcomes":[{"measure":"Achievement of Physical activity recommendations","description":"Proportion of patients in each arm of the study (intervention and control) who achieve physical activity recommendations.

At week 6, patients receive a scan dose of iodine I 131 followed by whole body scanning over 5 days. Beginning at week 7, patients undergo a treatment phase consisting of oral liothyronine sodium twice daily for 3 weeks, azacitidine subcutaneously daily for 10 or 20 days (weeks 7-11) and a low iodine diet on weeks 8-11. During week 11, patients undergo additional whole body scanning over 5 days followed by a therapeutic dose of iodine I 131. Patients achieving successful therapy receive 5 additional doses of azacitidine. Cohorts of 4 patients receive escalating doses of azacitidine until demonstrable radioiodine uptake is seen or the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) is determined. The MTD is defined as the dose preceding that at which 2 of 8 patients experience dose limiting toxicity. Patients are followed weekly for 8 weeks.
